newsitem.title: USA: Judge testy at pace of Oklahoma City bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: Judge testy at pace of Oklahoma City bombing trial.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial has showed signs of testiness at some defence questioning but legal experts predicted on Friday there would be no problem seating a jury to try defendant Timothy McVeigh.

With a 27th potential juror being quizzed as court resumed on Friday, it appeared the massive pre-trial publicity in the case -- including news reports that McVeigh had confessed to his attorneys -- was not going to be a major problem in finding a jury.

A handful of prospective jurors admitted to reading newspapers -- but only the sports pages. A few recalled seeing reports about McVeigh's alleged confession and all swore to U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch that since being called for duty they avoided hearing or reading about the case.

One man questioned on Friday said he saw a report about the alleged confession but gave it short shrift, adding: "I'd probably put that in line with what I'd see in the (supermaraket tabloid) National Enquirer ... It didn't seem credible to me."

Defence lawyers, who have denied the confession reports, said their greatest fear was that pre-trial publicity would make it impossible for McVeigh, 28, to get a fair hearing. At one point, they wanted the trial moved far away -- to Alaska or Hawaii.

McVeigh was formally charged with the "use of a weapon of mass destruction" and the murder of eight federal officials. A second defendant, his former Army buddy Terry Nichols, will be tried separately later. Both pleaded not guilty.

All jurors questioned so far vividly remembered April 19, 1995 -- the day a massive fuel and fertiliser bomb tore the glass face off the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people and injuring some 500 others. And many remember seeing McVeigh being paraded in an orange prison jumpsuit shortly after his arrest.
Matsch, famed for his short temper, was in a testy mood on Thursday, cutting off defence lawyers and even rephrasing a question for one of them to make it clear.

"We're far afield from the issues in this case," Matsch thundered at attorney Richard Burr when he asked a potential juror if he could imagine any method of political change in the United States other than elections. "I'd like you to focus on the issues here," he added.
When defence lawyer Mandy Welch tried to ask a Vietnam War veteran about his political views, including which party he belonged to, the judge snapped that the question was improper.

Later, when a bell started ringing in court, Welch interrupted her questioning to say: "Sorry, your honour, I thought I set something off." "Not yet," the glowering judge said, putting his face in his hands.
On Friday, the judge was in a better mood, making several jokes, although he chided a defence lawyer for continuing after saying he had asked his last question of a juror.
Jury selection moved slowly with lawyers and Matsch spending up to an hour and an half to question a prospective juror.

Denver legal expert Scott Robinson said that despite the slowness of the questioning, the trial seemed to be on the right track. "I've said all along that it will take three to four weeks to select a jury," he said.
A local TV station, KCNC, reported that as of Wednesday six jurors had been excused from service. The court has to find a pool of 64 jurors from which to choose 12 jurors and six alternates.
Total opposition to capital punishment is one reason a juror can be excused because the charges against McVeigh carry a possible death penalty.
One woman told the judge on Friday, "I personally don't feel I'd be able to live with a decision of saying someone should die or live." Questioning of her was cut short after she made that comment.
